claims.text: Rapid heating–cooling synthesis of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles commonly produces phase separation, elemental segregation, or non-uniform morphology because of kinetic trapping.
A brief dwell just below nucleation onset enhances atomic diffusion.
A slightly reduced initial heating rate is mechanistically equivalent to introducing a dwell below nucleation onset.
Enhanced atomic diffusion reduces local concentration gradients and improves elemental homogenization.
Additional diffusion time before nucleation prevents premature or heterogeneous nucleation.
Suppressing premature or heterogeneous nucleation favors a uniform single-phase solid solution over phase-separated or segregated microstructures.
The targeted single-phase solid solution is the thermodynamically favored state of these alloys.
Without sufficient homogenization, the alloy becomes trapped in a metastable, non-equilibrium state.
Increasing the number of constituent elements promotes more random mixing in nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to fixed compositions containing more than five noble metal elements under rapid thermal processing.
The dwell temperature must remain below nucleation onset while being high enough to promote appreciable diffusion.
Relative to a no-dwell control, the dwell intervention will produce a more uniform elemental distribution and fewer signs of phase separation, segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
Relative to a no-dwell control, the dwell intervention will produce a more uniform single-phase crystal structure.
An excessively high dwell temperature may cause early nucleation or decomposition.
High-temperature processing followed by rapid cooling can form single-solid-solution HEA nanoparticles by mixing the elements and suppressing secondary phases.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in elemental homogeneity and single-phase uniformity relative to the no-dwell control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline are described as typically phase-separated or segregated, while the predicted outcome says the intervention will 'maintain' a single-phase structure. The comparison is testable, but 'maintain' is inconsistent with a baseline that is not initially single phase.

The baseline characterizes standard rapid thermal cycles as typically yielding heterogeneous microstructures, whereas the mechanism frames the desired single phase as thermodynamically favored. The cited rapid-synthesis evidence instead describes the single solid solution as a non-equilibrium state preserved by rapid cooling, leaving the thermodynamic characterization internally poorly aligned with the stated processing rationale.
